I'm reconsidering whether "first target" might not mean placement order at all, but instead some other ordering — maybe by visitation order, proximity to the cube, or a separate numbering scheme entirely.

Since I can't access the episodes directly, proposing a speculative rule feels too risky. I'll commit nothing this round, provide a refusal with an explanation, and flag the hypothesis that the recorded target's identity may come from some other feature than placement order — something a future report should test by examining the recorded target's properties directly.

revision.refused: Nothing is committed this round. The report asks for nothing, and the two failed steps are the same mismatch seen in every round so far: the policy wrote the memory the rule prescribes, the annotator wrote the same value, and the subgoal followed from it; the recorded drop went to a target the forward count of the goal-named cube's demonstration placements does not name, and this time to a target the cube was never set down on at all (as once in round 1). The proposal from the failed steps, that an early set-down was skipped, was checked against the frames and found false, so no change to the placement-detection procedure is warranted; sharpening it would be a clause for a case the demonstration does not contain. Reversing the count to latest-first is refused for the fourth time: it fixed two and broke three in rounds 1 to 3 and would not explain this round's drops onto never-visited targets. Keying the rule on distractor cubes is refused again, as the round-3 report did not believe it was a cause. What the accumulated rounds now show is that the ordinal in the goal does not consistently index the order of the goal-named cube's releases: across four rounds the recorded target has been the ordinal-th placement forward, the ordinal-th placement backward, and a target the cube never touched. That pattern is a wrong hypothesis about what the ordinal names, not a wrong placement count, and no edit stated in terms of placements can settle it. The rule is left standing because it still fits the most recorded drops, and because a replacement needs a feature I cannot infer without the episodes. The annotator in the next round should, for each failed drop, record what else distinguishes the recorded target in the demonstration frames and in the first-step scene: its order in the scene's target listing, its position relative to the others (e.g. nearest to the robot, leftmost), whether any other cube or the button was set on or near it, and the order in which targets were first approached or covered by anything, so that one feature common to every recorded drop can be written as the rule for goal_target.
